description: Students in 3th year of engineering school
summary: Selene is an offline desktop application, built in C with raylib, that helps compare lunar south-pole landing sites and dates. It combines NASA LOLA elevation data and LROC imagery with an analytical ephemeris model. For every 200 m cell of a ~25 km zone, it computes when the Sun and Earth rise above the real terrain horizon, including lunar curvature. Users explore a 3D globe, a site view, a 360° ground view and a year-long analysis ranking candidate sites, with CSV export. It addresses the challenge by turning Sun and Earth geometry into mission metrics: sunlight for power, Earth visibility for direct communication, longest night, slope, roughness and proximity to shadowed ice. Users set priorities, mission length and start date, then see the best sites and dates. It serves two audiences: mission planners get engineer-level detail and exports, while students and the general public get an intuitive 3D interface, six languages and adjustable scale. This matters because near the south pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a few meters of terrain decide whether a lander has power or a radio link. Selene makes early site screening fast, transparent and offline, supporting Artemis-era planning and education. Results are early-screening estimates, not final mission design.
details:
What it does and how it works
Selene is an offline Windows desktop application that compares lunar south-pole landing sites and dates. A preparation tool cuts a 128 × 128 cell zone (about 25 km) out of NASA LOLA elevation data. For every cell, the program casts rays across the terrain to find the horizon profile, including lunar curvature. It then compares that horizon with the Sun and Earth positions over 30 days and a full year, using the apparent disk size of both bodies. Users explore a 3D globe, a site view, a “real view” with physically placed light and cast shadows, a 360° ground view, and an analysis tab. The analysis tab ranks candidate sites with a weighted score for energy, communication, thermal cycling (light/shadow cycles, not temperature), terrain and science (distance to permanently shadowed ice). It also finds the best start date and tests ranking stability with 30 perturbed weight sets. Results export to CSV.

Benefits
Early site screening becomes fast, transparent and independent of the internet. Every weight and constraint is visible and exported with the results.

Intended impact
Mission planners can shortlist sites quickly. Students and the general public can see why the poles are special: a few meters of terrain decide whether a lander has power or a radio link.

Tools

  • Languages and libraries: C (C11) with raylib for the interface and 3D rendering, Python with rasterio and numpy for data preparation, and sdefl/sinfl for compressed analysis files.
  • Data: NASA LOLA elevation, LROC imagery, and an analytical ephemeris model after Jean Meeus. It matched JPL Horizons within about 0.02° in our tests.
  • Software: MinGW-w64 and MSYS2, PyInstaller, NSIS installer, VS Code, GitHub.
  • Hardware: a standard Windows PC.
  • AI assistance: Claude, used as a coding assistant.

Creativity
Selene is a native, installable program rather than a web page. It serves two audiences at once (engineers and the public), runs in six languages added by plain text files (French, English, Spanish, Italian, Russian, Japanese), and offers metric or imperial units and interface scaling. Globe filters show illumination on a chosen date, elevation, deviation from the mean, and roughness.

Factors considered

  • Accuracy versus speed: 200 m cells and 6-hour steps in the annual analysis.
  • Known limits: boulders and small craters are invisible, and scoring weights are heuristic.
  • Practical constraints: offline reliability for classrooms and the field, public-domain data, and clear explanations of limitations. Reference frame differences are below 1 km.
  • Team: four people working within the hackathon’s time.
